title: Twitter Social Media: Complete Architecture
description: Design a Twitter-scale microblogging platform with hybrid fan-out timelines, Snowflake IDs, social graph caching, and trending topics.

data.text: Design a real-time microblogging platform like Twitter (X). The platform supports 350+ million monthly active users posting 500 million tweets daily (averaging 6,000 tweets/sec with peaks exceeding 150,000 tweets/sec during major events). The critical challenge is the Home Timeline: rendering an up-to-the-second stream of posts from hundreds of followed accounts in under 100ms, while efficiently handling high-follower accounts ("celebrity problem") without overwhelming system resources.

terms.definition: Injecting a new tweet ID directly into the Redis Home Timeline cache of every follower immediately upon creation. Read is O(1).
Generating the timeline dynamically when requested by fetching recent tweets from all followed users and merging them in memory. Write is O(1).
Pushing tweets to regular users' caches on write, but deferring celebrity posts (>25k followers) to merge dynamically on read.
A 64-bit globally unique, roughly time-ordered identifier composed of timestamp, machine ID, and sequence number.
A high-throughput distributed graph database specifically optimized for fast 1-hop follower/following lookups.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Post Tweets: Short text (up to 280 characters) with optional images, video clips, and polls
Follow / Unfollow: Follow accounts and maintain real-time follower/following relationship lists
Home Timeline: Display reverse-chronological or ranked stream of tweets from followed users
User Timeline: Display all historical tweets authored by a specific user profile
Interactions: Like, Retweet, Quote Tweet, and Reply with thread hierarchy
Search & Trends: Full-text search by keyword/hashtag and real-time regional trending topics
Notifications: Real-time alerts for mentions, likes, retweets, and new followers

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Scale: 500 million tweets/day; 6,000 writes/sec avg (150,000 peak); 600,000 timeline reads/sec
Latency: Sub-100ms P99 latency for Home Timeline retrieval
Consistency: Eventual consistency for timeline updates (up to 3-5 seconds lag is acceptable)
High Read-to-Write Ratio: ~100:1 read-to-write ratio (heavily read-dominant system)
Availability: 99.99% availability for timeline reading; 99.9% for tweet creation

data.text: The system uses a Hybrid Fan-out architecture. Normal users have their tweets pushed into follower timeline caches asynchronously via Kafka. Celebrities with tens of millions of followers do not fan-out on write; instead, their tweets are merged into the home timeline at query time.

data.text: Hybrid Timeline: Write vs Read Sequence

The hybrid fan-out model ensures ordinary tweets appear in follower timelines within milliseconds, while preventing a celebrity tweet (e.g., 100M followers) from executing 100M synchronous cache updates.

data.caption: Hybrid Timeline flow: Standard user fan-out on write vs Celebrity on-demand merge on read
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Alice as 👤 Normal User (Alice)
    actor Celeb as ⭐ Celebrity (10M Followers)
    actor Bob as 👤 Follower (Bob)
    participant API as 🚪 API Gateway
    participant Fanout as ⚡ Fanout Worker
    participant Graph as 👥 Social Graph
    participant Redis as ⚡ Redis Timeline Cache
    participant TimeSvc as 📖 Timeline Service

    Note over Alice, Redis: Scenario A: Normal User Posts Tweet
    Alice->>API: POST /tweet ("Hello world!")
    API->>Fanout: Async Publish TweetCreated (Alice, ID: 101)
    Fanout->>Graph: GetFollowers(Alice) -> [Bob, Charlie]
    Fanout->>Redis: LPUSH home:bob 101 (LTRIM 800)
    Note over Fanout, Redis: Tweet is already in Bob's cache!

    Note over Celeb, Redis: Scenario B: Celebrity Posts Tweet
    Celeb->>API: POST /tweet ("New album out!")
    API->>Fanout: Async Publish TweetCreated (Celeb, ID: 999)
    Fanout->>Fanout: Check Follower Count (>25,000: Celebrity)
    Fanout->>Redis: LPUSH user:celeb 999
    Note over Fanout: SKIP pushing to 10M followers' home caches!

    Note over Bob, TimeSvc: Scenario C: Bob Loads Home Timeline
    Bob->>API: GET /timeline/home
    API->>TimeSvc: GetHomeTimeline(Bob)
    TimeSvc->>Redis: LRANGE home:bob 0 50 (Get standard tweets)
    TimeSvc->>Graph: GetFollowedCelebrities(Bob) -> [Celeb]
    TimeSvc->>Redis: LRANGE user:celeb 0 10 (Get celeb's recent tweets)
    TimeSvc->>TimeSvc: Merge & Sort by Snowflake TweetID
    TimeSvc-->>API: Return Combined 50 Tweets
    API-->>Bob: Render Timeline (<80ms)

faqs.question: Why not use pure Fan-out on Read (Pull model)?
faqs.answer: In a pure pull model, every time an active user opens their timeline, the system must query hundreds of followed accounts, fetch their latest tweets, and run an in-memory k-way merge. At 600,000 read requests per second, this creates extreme read amplification and database exhaustion. Push pre-computes timelines so reads are simple O(1) Redis operations.

faqs.question: Why does the Celebrity cutoff point matter in Hybrid Fan-out?
faqs.answer: If an account has 50 million followers, pushing one tweet triggers 50 million Redis LPUSH writes. If 10 celebrities tweet within the same minute, the fan-out queue backs up with hundreds of millions of writes, delaying normal users' timeline updates. Hybrid keeps the fan-out queue lean by leaving high-degree nodes to on-read merging.

faqs.question: What is Twitter Snowflake and why is it used over UUID?
faqs.answer: Snowflake generates 64-bit integer IDs ordered by time: 41 bits for timestamp (milliseconds), 10 bits for machine/datacenter ID, and 12 bits for per-machine sequence. Because IDs are strictly increasing with time, databases (Cassandra/B-Trees) can insert them sequentially without page fragmentation, and timeline sorting is a simple integer comparison without date parsing.

faqs.question: How is the Home Timeline cached efficiently in Redis?
faqs.answer: Each user has a Redis List or Sorted Set containing at most 800 Tweet IDs (int64). Storing IDs instead of full tweet JSON saves memory (~6.4 KB per user). When the timeline is requested, the top 20-50 IDs are sliced, and the tweet text/author details are hydrated in batch via multi-get from a distributed Memcached cluster.

faqs.question: How do inactive users avoid wasting memory in Redis?
faqs.answer: Only active users (who opened Twitter in the last 14 days) keep their timeline in Redis. If an inactive user has not logged in, fan-out workers skip updating their cache. When the inactive user eventually returns, their timeline is rebuilt on-demand from the database.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Hybrid Fan-Out resolves the celebrity bottleneck: push for normal users, pull/merge for celebrities
Redis caches only 64-bit Tweet IDs (capped at 800), hydrating payload data in batch via Memcached
Snowflake IDs provide globally unique, 64-bit time-sortable identifiers without database coordination
Active-user eviction: only users active in the past 14 days have memory allocated in Redis timeline clusters
Stream processing (Apache Flink) computes real-time trending topics via sliding-window hashtag counts
data.takeaway: Twitter's high-read architecture succeeds by pre-computing timelines via asynchronous fan-out for 99% of accounts, while surgically handling high-follower celebrities through on-demand read-time merging.
